content_list.content_text: Cinema at once created and fed an appetite for spectacle, offering the chance to recreate the past, reimagine the present and envision the future. The pioneers of this art were not to be found in Hollywood, which at the time did not even exist as a center of film production, but in Europe. Among the most notable were the French filmmakers Georges Méliès (1861-1938), Charles Pathé (1863-1957) and Ferdinand Zecca (1864-1947).

The latter directed the one-minute short film A la conquête de l'air (Conquering the Skies, 1901), in which he appears flying over the Parisian neighborhood of Belleville in a bizarre flying machine. The film was made for the production company Pathé Frères, founded in 1896 by Charles Pathé and his brother Émile. In a nod to their origins as restaurant owners, they used a rooster, Le Coq, as their logo.

information.contentText: Logo of one of the most important production companies of all time, featuring the rooster Le Coq, present on its posters from the very beginning.

content_list.content_text: We can mention other names that were unknown until then: Thomas Edison (1847-1931), W.K.L Dickson (1854-1932), Louis Le Prince (1841-1890) and Francis Doublier (1878-1948). All of them contributed in some way to the creation of the so-called seventh art, and for that reason we cannot say it was created by a single person, nor does it have a precise date of birth. In 1884, George Eastman invented roll film. In the same decade, Thomas Edison and his assistant W. K. L. Dickson invented the kinetoscope. Many other inventions emerged in parallel or built upon earlier ones.

information.contentText: The Kinetoscope is a device for viewing films internally, invented by William Kennedy Laurie Dickson, chief engineer at Thomas Edison's Edison Laboratories, in 1891.

content_list.content_text: But one date went down in history: December 28, 1895, widely regarded by historians as the birth date of cinema. That night, at the Grand Café in Paris, they showed a short program of their documentary films to a paying audience; soon after came the now-famous L'Arrivée d'un train en gare de La Ciotat (The Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat, 1896).

After attending the first public screenings of the Lumière brothers' films in 1895, theater producer and magician Georges Méliès quickly recognized cinema's potential as a vehicle for illusion and fantasy. Méliès's signature was his love of illusionism, blending the fantastic with the macabre. The silent film L'Homme à la tête de caoutchouc (The Man with the Rubber Head, 1901) features Méliès as a scientist who attaches a rubber tube to his own severed head to inflate it with a bellows. The experiment is then repeated by one of his assistants, who inflates the head until it explodes.

information.contentTitle: The Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat
information.contentText: One of the first films in history to be shown to a paying audience. The camera was placed near the tracks, so that the train grew larger as it approached, until it seemed it would burst through the screen and into the room. Legend has it that people ducked, screamed or got up to leave.

content_list.content_text: In Le Voyage dans la Lune (A Trip to the Moon, 1902), the image of the rocket landing in the eye of the Moon is a typical example of Méliès's blend of the eccentric and the visceral. Yet despite all the fascinating cinematic innovations this filmmaker developed and explored, his films never managed to break free entirely from their theatrical origins.

In India, pioneering director D. G. Phalke (1870-1944), enchanted by one of the first film versions of the life of Christ, learned the rudiments of filmmaking in order to make Raja Harishchandra (1913). This elaborate period drama, based on Hindu mythology, marks the beginning of the Indian film industry.

quote.quote: If you've ever wondered where your dreams come from, you look around... this is where they're made.
quote.author: Georges Méliès - Hugo

content_list.content_text: Italy's film pioneers were drawn to the mythical and the spectacular. Dante's work proved a great source of inspiration, and L'Inferno (Dante's Inferno, 1911) is considered the country's first feature film.

In the United States, The Great Train Robbery (1903), directed by Edwin S. Porter (1870-1941), is considered the first American film with a narrative. Porter's innovative shooting and editing techniques, his location shots and the Western format made it extremely thrilling for audiences of the time. As technology advanced, directors were able to make longer films, sometimes turning to literature for inspiration.

information.contentText: This was one of the earliest known science fiction films. A part near the end was animated, which also makes it one of the first animated films.

content_list.content_text: As technology advanced, the length of films increased, making possible the emergence of serial films. One of the most successful examples of the format is the Fantômas series (1913-1914), divided into five parts and based on one of the most popular characters in French crime fiction, played by René Navarre (1877-1968). Directed by Louis Feuillade (1873-1926), each part ran about an hour and always ended on a cliffhanger. The prolific French director also made Les Vampires (The Vampires, 1915). The suspense techniques developed by Feuillade would later influence masters such as Fritz Lang (1890-1976) and Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980).

content_list.title: Serial Films
content_list.description:
Between 1908 and 1920, cinema developed through so-called serial films, or serials, which became the main attraction of movie houses. This innovation, however, was not an invention of cinema, since at the time, especially in France, biweekly installments of crime and adventure stories were popular and had spread throughout Europe. It was in France, therefore, that the serial was born, with Nick Carter in le roi des détectives, in 1908, based on those installments and directed by Victorin Jasset, an imaginative director who often improvised the script during shooting. Following the series' success, several imitations were made in Europe, such as Raffles and Sherlock Holmes in Denmark, and Nick Carter in Germany.

The most famous serial of the era, however, was Fantômas, by Louis Feuillade, adapted from the serialized novel by Pierre Souvestre and Marcel Allain.

Serial films reached the United States around 1912, with What Happened to Mary (1912), a co-production of Edison Studios Company and the magazine The Ladies World, the first American serial. While serials were playing in theaters, they were usually accompanied by the same story published in chapters in newspapers.

Serials proliferated, producing their masterpieces, such as The Million Dollar Mystery (1914), produced by the Thanhouser Film Corporation, which earned ten times its cost, and The Perils of Pauline, a Pathé / Hearst production starring Pearl White, who soon became an idol of young audiences.

Serials became very popular among children and young people in the first half of the 20th century, and film screenings, including in Brazil, were generally preceded by an episode of a serial until the '60s, as they were known back then. They were later acquired by TV channels and shown in weekly or daily episodes. Most were Westerns, but there was a wide range of genres: dramas, science fiction, espionage, jungle adventures, as well as book adaptations.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the article Seriado on Wikipedia

content_list.content_text: The opportunity to make longer films, the rise of the Hollywood studios and bigger budgets encouraged filmmakers to produce literary adaptations such as 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea (1916), directed by Stuart Paton (1883-1944) and based on the 1869 novel by Jules Verne, whose book The Mysterious Island (1874) was also adapted for the screen. Paton joined forces with two other British immigrants in the United States, the brothers John and George Williamson, to create the first film with some underwater sequences.

The appetite for spectacle continued to be explored in epics such as The Ten Commandments (1923) and Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ (1925), forming what would later be known as the sword-and-sandal genre. The latter proved a troubled and expensive production for Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, which had just completed its merger. To make the chariot race more exciting, the studio offered a $100 prize to the winner, and the terrible crash that resulted remained in the film's final cut. The spirit of pioneering director Georges Méliès can be glimpsed in these 1920s epics and, later, in the special effects created by Ray Harryhausen in the 1950s and 1960s. Filmmaking techniques grew more complex and narrative structures increasingly sophisticated, yet cinema's creative foundation — reinventing and reinterpreting reality — has remained a constant since its earliest days.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Carol King and Dominic Power, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

movies.title: A Trip to the Moon
movies.overview: Professor Barbenfouillis and five of his colleagues from the Academy of Astronomy travel to the Moon aboard a rocket propelled by a giant cannon. Once on the lunar surface, the bold explorers face the many perils hidden in the caves of the mysterious satellite.

movies.title: The Great Train Robbery
movies.overview: The clerk at the train station is assaulted and left tied by four men, then they rob the train threatening the operator. (They) take all the money and shoot a passenger when trying to run away. A little girl discovers the clerk tied and gives notice to the sheriff, who at once goes along with his men hunting the bandits.

movies.title: Conquering the Skies
movies.overview: A man flies his plane "Fend l'Air" over Paris.

movies.title: Raja Harishchandra
movies.overview: The first feature-length Indian film is based on the legend of Raja Harishchandra, recounted in the Ramayana and Mahabharata. It revolves around the noble and righteous king, Harishchandra, who first sacrifices his kingdom, followed by his wife and eventually his children to honour his promise to the sage Vishwamitra. Though, in the end, pleased by his high morals, the Gods restore his former glory, and further bestow him with divine blessings.

movies.title: Fantômas
movies.overview: A French silent saga which follows the exploits and crimes of the archvillain Fantômas, who commits crimes while eluding Inspector Juve's tireless persecution.

movies.title: Les Vampires
movies.overview: Two journalists attempt to uncover the truth behind the criminal organisation, known as The Vampires, who are terrorizing Paris.

movies.title: 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea
movies.overview: Captain Nemo has built a fantastic submarine for his mission of revenge. He has traveled over 20,000 leagues in search of Charles Denver - a man who caused the death of Princess Daaker. Seeing what he had done, Denver took the daughter to his yacht and sailed away.

movies.title: The Ten Commandments
movies.overview: The first part tells the story of Moses leading the Jews from Egypt to the Promised Land, his receipt of the tablets and the worship of the golden calf. The second part shows the efficacy of the commandments in modern life through a story set in San Francisco. Two brothers, rivals for the love of Mary, also come into conflict when John discovers Dan used shoddy materials to construct a cathedral.
